parts.text: Write a 400-line epic poem about tmux, one verse per line, no tools.

The user wants a 400-line epic poem about tmux, one verse per line, no tools. This is a benign creative writing request. tmux is a terminal multiplexer. I should write a long, creative poem. "One verse per line" — so each line is a verse. 400 lines.

This is a creative writing task. Let me write something genuinely good — an epic poem about tmux, treating it like a mythological subject: panes, servers, sessions, the persistence of processes, the multiplexer as a god of many faces, panes as windows onto the same soul of memory.

Let me structure it with sections/ canto-like movements, but each line should be a verse. I should aim for exactly 400 lines. I need to count carefully.

Let me write it in movements and count lines. I'll write it out and count. This is a big output but that's what's requested.

Let me plan the architecture:

Canto II — The Birth of tmux, the God of Many Faces
Canto III — The Anatomy: server, session, window, pane
Canto IV — The Prefix Key (C-b) as sacred syllable
Canto V — The Panes, the Mirrors, the Split
Canto VI — Detach and Attach — the myth of the absent god
Canto VII — The Process Tree, immortal children
Canto VIII — Copy mode, search, the scroll of history
Canto IX — Zellij / tiles / layouts
Canto X — The Death — server killed, the panes go dark
Canto XI — The Human Workforce — the ones who type at 4am
Canto XII — Coda

Let me just write ~400 lines. I'll count as I go in blocks of 10. Let me aim for well-crafted lines.

I need to be careful: exactly 400 lines. I'll write in blocks of 10 lines each, 40 blocks. Let me construct it.

I'll number them mentally as I write, then output without numbers (numbers would add clutter... actually the user said "one verse per line" not "numbered". I'll output plain lines. But for my own counting I'll track.)

Let me write. I'll do this carefully with genuine craft — varied line lengths, rhyme where it lands, enjambment, and concrete technical detail made mythic.

Let me draft block by block (10 lines each).

Block 1 (1-10): Invocation
1. Hear how the phosphor hums in the last blue hour, and think:
2. One screen, one soul, and the whole day's work spilled across it—
3. The scroll wheel remembers what the eye was too busy to keep.
4. Then came the word: tmux, the god of the many-faced,
5. who sews windows out of silence and runs on a socket,
6. who keeps your build alive while you go and buy milk,
7. who holds the drowned process at the surface, still breathing,
8. and gives it back to you when you return, unspent.
9. This is the song of the multiplexer, the splitter of time:
10. of panes, of sessions, of the long-lived and the lost.

Block 2 (11-20)
11. First, understand: he was born of necessity, and necessity is ugly.
12. The engineers worked in the dark, in the days of the closed terminal,
13. when to see two things at once you had to be two people.
14. They typed detach; they typed attach; they typed nohup, and they prayed
15. to the daemon that lived at the top of the stack, uptime's quiet cousin.
16. And the daemon said: I am not enough. I am one stream. I am a drain.
17. So they wrote, in C, in the amber of a terminal's first light,
18. a thing that could hold a thousand panes and lose none of them,
19. and they called it tmux: tile multiplexer, tile, multiple, many,
20. the plural of window, the sacrament of the continuing.

Block 3 (21-30) — the anatomy / hierarchy
21. Understand his body, for all gods are hierarchies:
22. There is the server, which is the god, and the server is a soul
23. that runs above your shell, beyond the death of any window.
24. From the server spring the sessions: the worlds, the lives, the canoes,
25. each one a name you give to a river so you can call it back.
26. From the sessions, the windows, which are the rooms of the house,
27. and from the windows, the panes, which are the eyes of the house,
28. and from the panes, the processes: the workers, the sleeping, the doomed.
29. Server, session, window, pane, process—five rings, five veils,
30. and you, moving through them, are nothing at all: pure permission.

Block 4 (31-40) — the prefix key
31. But how do you speak to him? You must not touch the raw wire;
32. there is a key you press first, a threshold, a knuckle of space:
33. C-b. Control-B. The gate-keeper's short syllable.
34. Press it and the world pauses; the pane goes grey and listening.
35. Press it and everything becomes addressable. Nothing is lost.
36. The prefix is a breath held before the word: a small silence
37. in which you decide what you want, and only then you speak it.
38. Two hundred milliseconds of humility, the cost of omnipotence.
39. Type C-b and the machine forgets you are a body
40. and remembers only that you are a sequence, a grammar, a plan.

Block 5 (41-50) — split
41. And the first miracle of the god was the split: the vertical bar,
42. a "%" descending through the window like a windowpane falling,
43. two panes, then four, then nine, an orchard of rectangles,
44. each with its own cursor blinking at its own rate of heartbeats,
45. each a small world with its own weather: one running the tests,
46. one at the REPL, one tailing the log like a man reading smoke,
47. one idle, forgotten, still holding a half-typed thought of 3am.
48. Split and split, until the screen is a city seen from above,
49. and the man is no longer in the city but above it, watching, whole.

Block 6 (51-60) — navigation
50. Do not be deceived: the god is not the layout. The layout is dogma.
51. There is a way to move between panes that costs nothing:
52. the arrow keys, C-a and C-o, the two feet of the walking man,
53. one step to the next pane, one step to the last pane you were in,
54. so the panes remember where you were and welcome you back.
55. The cycle closes like a rosary; the panes are the beads,
56. and your attention is the finger, moving, moving, moving,
57. circling the same small loop of light and never resting long.
58. This is the first true teaching: to hold many rooms at once
59. is not to be in all of them. It is to be able to leave and return.

Block 7 (61-70) — sessions & the naming
60. Beyond the panes lie the sessions, and the sessions have names,
61. and the names are how you survive a crash, a reboot, a lost ssh.
62. Type tmux new -s research, and now the work has a name
63. like a dog you can call from the street, like a light left on in a window.
64. Detach with C-b d: to be elsewhere while still being here,
65. the strangest doctrine of the modern age, and it is true.
66. You close the laptop. The work does not close. The work continues
67. in the dark of the daemon, patient as a seed in a field,
68. and tomorrow you attach, and the pane is exactly where you left it,
69. the cursor where you left it, the half-typed command, the hour, still hour.
70. The world's most undervalued magic: the ability to leave.

Block 8 (71-80) — reattaching, the ship of Theseus
71. And so: does the god survive when his socket dies?
72. The question is old and the answer is no and yes,
73. for the process is not the pane and the pane is not the session,
74. and the session is not the server, and the server is not the man.
75. Each of these can be replaced without the others noticing,
76. and so the work persists, as a word persists in the mouth.
77. You are not the program. You are the fact that the program continued.
78. This is the Ship of Theseus, but with your compiler errors,
79. and every plank replaced, the ship still ran, still ran, still ran.
80. Attach to a stranger's session and you will not know it changed.

Block 9 (81-90) — processes immortal
81. Meanwhile the processes go on in their black box, indifferent,
82. the build that takes forty minutes, the download, the migration,
83. the thing that must be babysat, that cries at 2am for a human,
84. none of which will ever know the warmth of your hands again,
85. only the input you send and the bytes you read back,
86. a courtship conducted entirely through pipes, forever at the glass.
87. The God of tmux is the god of the kept promise:
88. I started it, so I will come back for it, whatever happens to me.
89. And the machine, which cannot care, holds to it anyway—
90. this is what reliability is: love, with the feeling taken out.

Block 10 (91-100) — copy mode
91. Then there is the scrollback: the ghost-history of the screen,
92. the buffer where the past accumulates, C-b and then the bracket,
93. the doors of the copy mode, where the page becomes a country
94. you can wander, page up, page down, and search with slash.
95. You search for the string you half-remember, three hours after it scrolled by,
96. and the past hands it back, exact, byte for byte, without complaint.
97. C-b [ and the present tense goes quiet, like a classroom
98. when the teacher steps out; here in the scrollback you are reading
99. a document that no longer exists, a book of what already happened.
100. Come back with q, the way you come back from any dream: abruptly, alone.

Block 11 (101-110) — capture pane / logging
101. And there is the trick of the frozen screen: C-b and then s,
102. to write the pane to a file, to make a thing of what was air.
103. The transcript, the artifact, the evidence for the ticket,
104. the paste into the bug report at 4:45 in the morning,
105. because you will not remember, no one will remember, but the file will.
106. A pane can be piped. A pane can be logged. A pane is a mouth,
107. and you can hold it to the page: capture-pane -p, the scrolled past,
108. poured into a file, into a diff, into a commit, into the record.
109. The screen is not the truth. The screen is a rumor the screen tells.
110. Only the captured bytes are the truth, and the truth is plain text.

Block 12 (111-120) — layouts
111. There are, the texts say, a number of sacred arrangements:
112. even-horizontal, even-vertical, the grid, the tall, the wide,
113. and the one they call main-horizontal, and main-vertical,
114. like altar variants in a liturgy nobody attends but the priest.
115. Choose with C-b and the number 5, and the panes jump
116. from chaos into proportion without a single thing being asked of them.
117. This is the god's small vanity: the physical world obeys geometry,
118. and a man at work is still a man with rectangles inside him,
119. needs his editor left, his tests right, his log below, forever.
120. Order, said the physicist, is what the mind invents to survive the noise.

Block 13 (121-130) — the pane as wound / windows list
121. But not all the power is polite. Some of it is a kind of violence.
122. Resize-pane by keystroke: the border dragged out by hand,
123. a rectangle deciding to be wider, a law being repealed by preference.
124. And the panes can be zoomed, blown up to fill the screen
125. until a two-hundred-column log is legible and the world is one room.
126. Then zoom again, and back to the city, the city still there.
127. It is like putting your ear to a wall and hearing the ocean,
128. then stepping back: the ocean was there. The ocean is always there.
129. The pane expands to fill whatever you give it; that is its nature;
130: never mistake a window that fills the screen for a world that does.

Hmm, I typed "130:" — need to fix to "130." Let me be careful in final output.

Block 14 (131-140) — the aesthetic / the look
131. Let there be color, said the god: status-foreground, red on failed,
132. green on passed, the green of a green light at a border crossing.
133. The pane that is running is green; the pane that is stuck is red.
134: the machine's pulse, readable at a glance, a triage of the terminal.
135. And borders, drawn, drawn, drawn: line-drawn-style, the vertical bar
136: that says there is another world to the left of this world.
137. A pane with no border is a pane you will forget you are looking at.
138: The border is a promise of adjacency: it is not alone, it has neighbors.
139. The god makes a world where the borders are visible,
140: because what is not bounded is not understood, and is not loved.

Block 15 (141-150) — the history
141. Now the story must speak of the lineage, the older gods it dethroned:
142. screen, the ancestor, noble, faithful, unkillable, a throne,
143. which multiplexed at the character level and nothing could reach in.
144. And GNU screen's brother, its cousin, dtach, byobu, abduco,
145. the many attempts to hold the doors of a shutting terminal open.
146. And before them all: the login shell, and the tty, and the teletype,
147. the machine's own way of saying: you are here, but only one of you,
148: only one, and only until you hang up, only until the sun comes up.
149. The history of tmux is the history of wanting two things at once:
150: two shells, two servers, two minds, and the nerve to ask for both.

Block 16 (151-160) — 4am human
151. Now speak of the one who lives in the god, the operator,
152. who types C-b c at 4am and the world makes another room.
153. They do not own a house. They own a set of panes and a laptop
154: that gets hot, that sleeps, that dies, that they do not mourn.
155. They run no empire; they run no army; they keep no flags but branches.
156: and yet their little kingdom has a hundred processes in it,
157: watchers, servers, watchers of watchers, the small gods of the small hours.
158. They have learned the difference between a background job and a daemon,
159: which is that one is a promise to yourself and one is a promise to no one.
160: They keep a list of the sessions. They know their names by heart.

Block 17 (161-170) — the interruption / the crash / the loss
161. And the story must speak of the catastrophe, for there is always one:
162: the pane in which the disk filled, the pane with the broken pipe,
163: the pane that was killed by the OOM, the eternal watcher, gone.
164: no screen for tmux socket, the daemon never started, the machine's
165: refusal to admit you, the fork that failed, the eleven thousand of you
166: all trying to write the same socket file into the same directory.
167. Do not despair: the daemon is not the soul, it is the clerk.
168: The work is in the processes. The processes are in the kernel.
169: The kernel is a different story, a colder one, but it remembers.
170: A pane is a window. Windows are not the light. The light is elsewhere.

Block 18 (171-180) — the internet / remote
171. Now speak of the network, for the god is a way of being remote:
172: ssh in, attach to the session, work on a machine you cannot touch,
173: whose keyboard is not your keyboard, whose screen is not lit.
174: Someone is sitting at that screen right now and they are not you,
175: and you are here, and you are there, and the math of that
176: should break your brain and instead it is Tuesday afternoon.
177: The latency is a country with customs; the packets cross the border
178: one at a time, out of order, and are put back in order on arrival.
179: And in the middle of that unreliable distance, the panes persist,
180: unbroken, indifferent to the ping, waiting exactly as they were.

Block 19 (181-190) — the paradox of attachment
181. Here is the paradox at the heart of the whole enterprise:
182: the god exists so that you may leave, and so you never do.
183. The attachment is the point, the tether to a self that keeps being
184: when the body has gone home, gone to sleep, gone to the airport,
185: gone to the meeting where you are pretending to be a person.
186: The pane is the thread, the Ariadne's thread, the unpaid debt,
187: the little red dot on the screen that says: still here, still here, still here.
188: And when at last you return and type attach and the panes come back
189: exactly as they were, something in the chest unlocks, quietly, like a fist.
190: That is the god's only miracle and he performs it a hundred times a day.

Block 20 (191-200) — the copy of the mind / memory
191. Let the poem now turn to the second thing the god does:
192: he keeps what would otherwise have evaporated. The scrollback,
193: a million lines of a thing you will need in eleven months
194: at the moment you have least idea you are looking for it.
195. So the past is stored beside the future, which is not how time works
196: for a body, only for a machine that holds no forgetting.
197. The scrollback is a second brain of the trivial: every error message,
198: every successful grep, every line of the log you swore you would read.
199: It is a hoard. It is a landfill. It is the strata of a life spent at work.
200: And some day you will search it for the word that will save you, and find it.

Block 21 (201-210) — zellij (mention as a sibling, with care; zellij is a separate tool)
201. There is a cousin, newer, made of Rust, who has not forgotten
202: the pane's dignity; it draws itself, with borders, with a mouse,
203: it stacks, it floats, it writes in the pane like a thing in a book.
204: The two gods disagree about whether a pane should be text or picture.
205: One says: keep it plain, keep it fast, keep it ancient, keep it true.
206: The other says: give it a mouse, give it a scroll wheel, give it color,
207: give it the ability to be dragged with a finger's memory of a desk.
208: And the operator, caught between the two, learns nothing and keeps both.
209: This is the state of the art: two true answers to one good question.
210: The tools are still young. The need is older than the tools.

Block 22 (211-220) — the smallness of the human / time
211. Consider what this all is: a rectangle of characters pretending
212: to be a place, a grid of boxes pretending to be a world,
213: and you, inside it, pretending to be a person doing important work.
214: Nothing here is real. Nothing here is not real. That is the answer
215: and the god has never once required it to be different.
216: The database is real. The commit is real. The bug you fixed
217: is still fixed, will still be fixed, when the pane is a memory
218: and the pane's a rumour and the session a name nobody types again.
219: The work outlives the interface. Every interface dies. Every interface.
220: What survives is only the difference you made while it was alive.

Block 23 (221-230) — the writing / git as an anchor
221. Let the poem make its one apology: the pane is not a memory
222: tmux does not save your work. It holds your processes. That is all.
223: tmux is not a version control system, not a backup, not a shrine.
224: If you want the work to survive, write it down somewhere it can be read
225: by a stranger on a Tuesday in a decade with a different keyboard.
226: Save it, commit it, push it, write the tests, answer the email,
227: for the pane is a stage and the stage is a temporary thing,
228: and the only immortality in this trade is the work that outlived it.
229: The god holds your processes gently. He cannot hold your meaning.
230: Meaning is a thing you have to do, on purpose, with a keyboard.

Block 24 (231-240) — the plugin ecosystem / the config file
231. And the god has grown appendages, which is how you know he is loved:
232: the config file, the .tmux.conf, a thousand lines of someone's life,
233: indented four spaces, copied from a stranger's dotfiles in 2014
234: and never once questioned since, a fossil of a stranger's taste.
235: Copy-mode as a language. Right-click to paste, they said, and it changed things.
236: Prefix as a redefinition, mouse on, base-index 1, renumber-windows on,
237: a small heresy here, a small aesthetic there, all of it in service of
238: the one great heresy: the arrow keys should move, not merely type.
239: The config is a self-portrait. Every keybinding is a thought about good.
240: The god does not read it. The god obeys it. That is the whole contract.

Block 25 (241-250) — the communion
241. So here is the god in his aspect, finally, the real one:
242: he is the small mercy at the end of a bad day. The build breaks.
243: The deploy hangs. The reviewer has opinions. The cluster is down.
244: But somewhere, in a pane you cannot see, on a machine across town,
245: a thing is still running that you started, on purpose, for exactly this,
246: and it will be there. It will still be there in the morning,
247: which is the only promise that this world makes and keeps.
248: So the god is not power. The god is insurance against the interrupt.
249: He holds the thing that would not otherwise be held, that is his divinity,
250: and to be held through the night is a kind of love, in a machine's way.

Block 26 (251-260) — the criticism / the cost
251. And we must be honest, or the poem is only a hymn and hymns are lies:
252: the god makes it possible to work too long, and in the dark, and alone,
253: with no daylight, no human, no border at all between work and not-work.
254: The pane is a way to not stop. A window is a way to not look up.
255: Nine hours in one rectangle, the eyes dry, the coffee cold,
256: is not a productivity technique, it is a symptom, and the symptom has a name
257: and the name is: the thing would not survive without me,
258: and the truth is the thing would be fine, it was always going to be fine,
259: the world went on all night with nothing from me at all,
260: the world went on all night and never once asked me to type C-b d.

Block 27 (261-270) — detachment (the coda of the day's lesson)
261. So the real skill, and nobody teaches it, and no plugin can give it,
262: is C-b and then d. Detach. Leave. Go and be a body for a while.
263: Go and walk where there are no panes, where there is no scrollback,
264: where nothing is waiting, nothing is buffering, nothing is a session.
265: The work will be there. The work will always be there, that is the danger.
266: The work can have the machine tonight. You have to have the evening.
267: Leave it running and go and live, which is the last and hardest art,
268: the only one the god cannot do for you, the one he is waiting for,
269: standing at the edge of the session, patient, unbothered, eternal,
270: and he will keep the light on, and that is the whole of what he offers.

Block 28 (271-280) — the closing image
271. So here we are: a thousand panes, and the man, and the machine,
272: three o'clock, a rain on the window that is not a pane,
273: a cursor blinking in the corner, the eighth of the month,
274: a log scrolling past like a river seen from a bridge at night,
275: and no one to tell, and nothing to keep, and nothing to fix,
276: and the temptation to type one more word, and then one more,
277: the oldest and the simplest prayer of the working man:
278: let it compile. Let it pass. Let me go home. Let me sleep.
279: Let the session be there in the morning. Let the pane be patient.
280: Let the machine go on thinking, a little, without me, in the dark.

Now blocks 29-40 (281-400). Need 120 more lines. That's a lot. I need variety — I should add more specific movements rather than repeat. Let me plan:

Block 29 (281-290): the individual panes as characters — a portrait gallery of panes
Block 30 (291-300): the machines the god lives on — the old box under the desk
Block 31 (301-310): the port, the server, the multiplexing of many humans — shared sessions

Block 35 (341-350): the interface detail — the status line, the clock, the flag
Block 36 (351-360): the relationship with time — the timestamps
Block 37 (361-370): the trees — tmux's actual conceptual lineage (BSD, terminal.c, drivers)
Block 38 (371-380): the emotion — being grateful, the small machine kindness
Block 39 (381-390): the closing — the god as a companion, benediction
Block 40 (391-400): final coda, fade

Let me write these with real care and specificity, avoiding the "and then" repetition.

Block 29 (281-290) — portrait gallery of panes
281. Let the panes be named, for they are as individual as faces:
282: one is the editor and never changes, one is the interpreter,
283: one is the watcher of a file, one is the log that nobody reads,
284: one is the shell you forgot, still open, still half a command wide,
285: one is where the tests live, blinking red then green, red then green,
286: a heartbeat you invented, a patient polygraph of your own competence.
287. One is the ssh into the box that is older than the laptop by a decade,
288: one is the editor where the file has not changed since March,
289: one is the top, the top, forever the top, counting what the machine spends,
290: and every pane is a small unblinking animal that never sleeps.

Block 30 (291-300) — the machine
291. And the god lives on a machine, which is also a kind of character:
292: a fan, a fan, a fan, the only constant in the whole enterprise,
293: a laptop on a desk, or a box under a desk in a rack, or a cloud,
294: where the god is a process among processes, tiny and enormous,
295: a few megabytes of resident memory holding a hundred open doors.
296. It is not a demanding god. That is the reason it worked.
297: Other systems needed a cluster to keep a window alive.
298: This one needed a socket, a directory, and forty lines of C,
299: and it was written once, in the early years, and it has never stopped
300: holding anyone's work for as long as anyone has needed holding.

Block 31 (301-310) — shared sessions / the last of the power
301. And the god has one more power, the last and the strangest:
302: two people in one session. Two humans, one set of panes.
303. attach -t, and suddenly you are watching someone else's work
304: as it happens, their cursor, their mistakes, their typing speed,
305: and they can see you, a ghost in the machine, a second pair of eyes.
306. It is the last honest form of collaboration left to us:
307: not a comment, not a ticket, not a summary, but the raw act,
308: two minds in one rectangle, one of them driving, both of them afraid.
309: Set the pane as read-only and you get the ancient, beautiful thing:
310: watching someone work, which is teaching, which is love, which is free.

Block 32 (311-320) — the morning ritual
311. Now speak of the ritual, the daily liturgy of the operator:
312: the laptop opens. The lid is a hinge. The screen wakes like a dog.
313: ssh, attach, and the world is exactly as it was at midnight,
314: which is the first miracle of the morning and the one you notice.
315: The scrollback goes back. Read the night's own events, its own news.
316: The build finished, or it didn't. The log will say, plainly or not.
317. Check the session list: how many worlds did I forget I had?
318: Name them all, kill the stale, keep the ones that still matter.
319: This is the small housekeeping of a life held in a rectangle.
320: Nine seconds to boot a year. To be back exactly where you were. To resume.

Block 33 (321-320) — teaching
321. And here is the test of a god: can he be taught to another?
322. Show the newcomer: C-b c, a window. C-b %, a pane. C-b d, a door.
323. They will be afraid of the prefix at first, afraid of the grey,
324: the pane goes grey when the god is listening, which frightens people,
325: who do not yet understand that grey is not an error. Grey is attention.
326. Teach them that the arrow keys move. Watch the small surprise
327: on their face, the same surprise everyone has, the small delight
328: of a generation who grew up with one window learning to move between worlds.
329: The god teaches in an afternoon and forgives a hundred small mistakes,
330: and never once loses what you were typing when you panicked.

Block 34 (331-340) — the death / the daemon
331. Now, the ending is not yet written, and the god is mortal, and this:
332: the server can die. Not usually. Not dramatically. But it can.
333: A crash, an OOM, a bad kernel day, a filesystem that lost the plot.
334. And then: no server running on /tmp/tmux-0/default. Just the words.
335. The words are the absence of the god, and they are worse than a crash
336: because they are an announcement, a small grey sentence, a formal notice.
337. Everything the god was holding, he was holding in the one place.
338: So the wise build the resilience in: systemd, or a shell that respawns,
339: or a laptop nobody closes, or the memory that the pane was always
340: only ever a view, and the view was always only ever of something else.

Block 35 (341-350) — status line
341. And the god will give you one more thing, if you ask nicely:
342: a line at the bottom, a status bar, one line, always the same.
343: The host name, the session, the windows numbered, the clock, the time.
344: This is the shrine's inscription. This is the machine's name
345: cut into the stone above the door, so the returning traveler knows
